text: Every command in Lessons 21 through 23 assumed the CLI or the Az module was already installed on your machine. Azure Cloud Shell removes that requirement entirely — a terminal that runs inside the Azure Portal, or at shell.azure.com, with nothing to install, because Microsoft runs the shell for you on a temporary machine behind the scenes. You pick Bash or PowerShell when you first open it, and both come with the exact same tools from this chapter already installed.

The machine running your shell is temporary and gets torn down after you close the session — but your files aren't. The first time you launch Cloud Shell, Azure creates a small Azure Files share, typically around 5 gigabytes, and mounts it as your home directory automatically. Anything you save there is still there the next time you open Cloud Shell, days later, even though the compute underneath is brand new every session. Worth knowing: it also disconnects after roughly 20 minutes of inactivity.

Here's the actual point of a script instead of one-off commands: doing the same thing across every item in a list, without typing the command once per item. In Bash, a for loop over az group list, filtered with Lesson 21's query and output tsv, prints every resource group and then everything inside each one.

The identical job in PowerShell: a foreach loop over Get-AzResourceGroup, using Lesson 23's cmdlets, listing every group and then every resource inside it with Get-AzResource. Same result, same underlying idea — a list the loop iterates over one item at a time — just the Bash or PowerShell syntax layered on top.

Cloud Shell is the right call when you're on someone else's machine or want zero setup. Your own local install is the right call for anything long-running or meant to run unattended on a schedule, since Cloud Shell's timeout and temporary compute make it a poor fit for that. Most administrators use both. Next, Chapter 7 turns to watching what these resources are actually doing, starting with Azure Monitor and metrics basics.
